title: Al-Muqsit, the Equitable
tomorrow: Saturday, one wall, a lot of paint. who shows up?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram, and an apology taken without shrinking anyone. The line: majesty and honor. Sorry has been said. Now comes the harder part: the bill.

A group project. One person made half the slides, one made none, and the grade is shared. Fair can mean everyone gets the same, or it can mean everyone gets what they put in, and that argument shows up everywhere from group chats to courtrooms. Yesterday's question: what's fair when the one who wronged you is thirteen? Full price? A free pass? Today's Name lives in the space between.
screen: `ONE DID HALF. ONE DID NONE.` → `FULL PRICE, OR A FREE PASS?` → `THE SPACE BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Al-Muqsit, the Equitable: the One who gives each their due, no thumb on the scale. The Qur'an tells believers, in Pickthall's words: "let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly." And elsewhere: "Lo! Allah loveth the equitable." Notice what the first verse names as the danger. Not ignorance. Anger. The moment you most want the scale to tip is the moment it has to stay level. Now a neighbor. Jews and Christians read a line in Leviticus, in the King James words: "thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour." That's the shared thing, and it's close: justice that refuses to lean. And here's the surprising part to tell a friend tonight. Leviticus doesn't only warn against favoring the powerful. It warns against favoring the poor, too. Even sympathy isn't allowed to tilt the verdict. The honest difference: Leviticus names status as the pull, poor or mighty, while the Qur'an's verse names hatred of a people. Each tradition is watching a different hand reach for the scale. So for a thirteen-year-old with a spray can, equity isn't full price or a pass. It's a share he can actually carry.

segments.voice: Pick one person you're finding it hard to be fair to this week. Name, in one honest sentence, what fair would look like, and then name what tilts you: anger, liking them, old history. Decide one thing you'll do when you feel the tilt, and hold that plan quietly through the sit.
